title: RBI Urges Savers to Search Old Accounts on the UDGAM Portal
summary: The Reserve Bank of India is urging people to search for forgotten deposits on its UDGAM portal, which covers 30 banks and lets savers and heirs find and claim balances moved to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund after 10 years of inactivity.
description:
The Reserve Bank of India has been encouraging people to look for forgotten money in old bank accounts through a search portal called UDGAM, short for Unclaimed Deposits, Gateway to Access Information. The portal lets savers and the families of deceased account holders check, in one place, whether banks hold dormant balances in their names. This article explains how unclaimed deposits are defined, what happens to the money, how the portal works, and how a person can claim a balance, using reporting from Business Today dated July 1, 2026 and from the Free Press Journal on the RBI's awareness campaign. It is a general guide based on public reporting and is not legal or financial advice. Readers should confirm details with their bank and the RBI.

What counts as unclaimed

According to Business Today, under RBI rules a savings or current account balance that has been inoperative for 10 years or more counts as an unclaimed deposit, as does a fixed deposit that has gone unclaimed for 10 years after maturity. The article's list of covered items also includes recurring and cumulative deposits left unclaimed after maturity, outstanding demand drafts and pay orders, unclaimed NEFT and unreconciled ATM credits, and other balances specified by the RBI. It also names items such as margin money, security deposits, bankers' cheques and undrawn prepaid card balances. The reports we reviewed do not give a total value of unclaimed deposits, so this article does not state one.

Where the money goes

Banks transfer unclaimed balances to the RBI's Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, known as the DEA Fund, which has been maintained since May 2014. The transfer happens on the last working day of the month after 10 years of continuous inactivity or unclaimed status. The important point is that the transfer does not end the depositor's ownership. The depositor, or the legal heirs, can claim the money at any time through the original bank, and there is no time limit for claiming money transferred to the fund. Interest-bearing deposits continue to earn interest under RBI guidelines. The bank pays the eligible interest to the claimant first and then seeks reimbursement from the fund.

How the UDGAM portal works

UDGAM is the RBI's centralised search platform at udgam.rbi.org.in. Business Today reports that it covers 30 participating banks. An individual first registers with a name and mobile number. A search then uses the account holder's name, the bank and one or more identifiers such as PAN, passport number, voter ID, driving licence or date of birth. Businesses can search with the entity name together with PAN, Corporate Identification Number, authorised signatory or date of incorporation. If identity details are not available, the article says an address-based search is possible.

The portal does not release money. It shows which bank holds an unclaimed deposit so that the person can approach that bank. Savers should note that banks outside the participating list will not appear in the search, so a person who suspects an account at another bank may need to contact it directly.

The claim process

The steps reported are simple. First, search on the UDGAM portal or on the bank's own website. Second, visit any branch of the bank concerned, which does not have to be the branch where the account was opened. Third, submit the prescribed claim form with valid KYC documents. The documents accepted include Aadhaar, passport, voter ID and driving licence. Fourth, the bank verifies the claim. Fifth, the bank pays the money, plus interest where it applies. Legal heirs may need extra documents, such as a death certificate and proof of relationship, and readers should ask the bank which ones it needs. Our sources did not list these.

The RBI campaign

The Free Press Journal reported that the RBI and banks ran a nationwide awareness campaign titled Jankaar Baniye, Satark Rahiye, which roughly means be informed and stay alert. Special camps were held across districts between October and December 2025 to help customers and legal heirs gather documents and begin claims. The campaign encouraged people to check for forgotten deposits of their own and of family members. Reports said the RBI has also asked banks to simplify claim procedures and help customers verify ownership.

How to avoid the problem

The RBI advises customers to review old accounts, update nominee details and keep KYC records current. A few practical habits help. Keep a list of every bank account and fixed deposit, including those opened for old jobs. Make at least one transaction a year on savings accounts to keep them active. Tell family members where accounts are held and who the nominee is. When closing a job, move the salary account to a standard savings account and keep it operative.

A caution about scams

Because the portal asks for personal details, readers should use only the official address named above or the websites of their banks. Callers or messages that ask for payment to release unclaimed money are not part of the process described in the reports. Our sources did not mention any fees, so readers should ask their bank before paying anything.

What to watch next

Readers can check whether more banks are added to UDGAM and whether the RBI repeats its camps. The RBI publishes announcements on its website, and banks list their own unclaimed deposits on their sites. This article summarises public reporting and is not financial advice.
source_name: Business Today (July 1, 2026); Free Press Journal (November 9, 2025); Reserve Bank of India campaign materials as reported
image_alt: Coins and savings representing unclaimed deposits (illustrative)
key_points: The RBI's UDGAM portal, at udgam.rbi.org.in, lets people search for unclaimed deposits across 30 participating banks in one place, after registering with a name and mobile number.

Savings or current account balances inoperative for 10 years, and fixed deposits unclaimed for 10 years after maturity, are moved to the RBI's Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, but the depositor or legal heirs keep the right to claim at any time.

To claim, a person searches on UDGAM, visits any branch of the relevant bank, submits a claim form with valid KYC documents such as Aadhaar, passport, voter ID or driving licence, and receives the money with interest where applicable.
Interest-bearing deposits continue to earn interest under RBI guidelines, and the bank pays the claimant first and then seeks reimbursement from the fund.
The RBI has advised customers to review old accounts, keep nominee details and KYC records current, and ran special unclaimed-asset camps across districts from October to December 2025.
why_it_matters: Money forgotten in an old salary account, a matured fixed deposit or an account of a deceased relative can sit untouched for years. A single search portal and a clear claim process make it easier for families to recover their own money, and updating nominee and KYC details can prevent the problem in future.

title: MAS Proposes Protected Cell Companies for Insurance Risk Transfer
summary: On July 7, 2026 the Monetary Authority of Singapore opened a consultation, closing August 7, on a Protected Cell Company framework that would let one legal entity run several ring-fenced cells for captive insurance, insurance-linked securities and sovereign risk pools.
description:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore, the country's central bank and financial regulator, published a consultation paper on July 7, 2026 proposing a new type of company for insurance and risk transfer: the Protected Cell Company, or PCC. Comments on the proposal were invited until August 7, 2026. MAS says the framework is intended to support the growth of alternative risk transfer solutions and to strengthen Singapore's position as a risk management hub. This article explains what a PCC is, what MAS proposes, and why the idea matters, using the MAS media release and a summary of the consultation paper by the law firm Rajah & Tann Asia. A proposal is not yet law, and the final rules may differ.

What a Protected Cell Company is

A PCC is a single legal entity that has a central part, called the Core, and one or more Cells. The key feature is that each Cell's assets and liabilities are legally separate from those of the other Cells and from the Core. If one Cell suffers losses, creditors of that Cell can pursue only that Cell's assets, and the other Cells are not exposed. The Core provides central governance and oversight. According to the law firm summary, neither the Core nor the Cells would have their own legal personality, since they form parts of one company, and a PCC would always have at least one Cell.

MAS describes the problem the structure is meant to solve. Today, a sponsor that wants to keep the capital, assets and liabilities of different risk programmes apart usually has to set up a separate legal entity, such as a special purpose vehicle, for each one. The cost and effort of doing so can discourage use. A PCC would let several programmes sit in one company while remaining separate in law.

The planned uses

The consultation names three initial uses. The first is captive insurance, in which a company insures its own risks through a subsidiary. A PCC could host a captive with several self-insurance programmes, each in its own Cell, or operate as a rent-a-captive, in which client companies use Cells within a facility run by a service provider rather than forming their own captive. The second is insurance-linked securities, or ILS, in which insurers raise capital from investors by issuing instruments tied to insurance risks. MAS says Cells could be used to issue ILS without creating a new special purpose vehicle for each deal, which would suit arrangements such as sidecars and collateralised reinsurance. The third is sovereign risk pools, which are multi-country or multi-participant arrangements, such as pools used to finance disaster risk.

Why MAS is doing this

MAS pointed to a protection gap. Citing Swiss Re Institute data from 2025, it said natural disasters caused about US$65 billion in economic losses across Asia in 2025, and more than 90% of that was uninsured. Alternative risk transfer, which covers captives, ILS and pools, is one way to bring more capital and more risk-sharing into that gap. The plan was announced by Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong at the Association of Banks in Singapore annual dinner on June 25, 2026, ahead of the consultation.

What the proposal says on segregation

According to the Rajah & Tann summary, the proposal contains detailed rules to make the ring-fencing work. Assets and liabilities would have to be recorded against either the Core or a specific Cell. The assets of one Cell could not be used to pay the liabilities of another, and creditors could pursue only the assets of the relevant Core or Cell. Contract terms inconsistent with segregation would be void.

When a PCC deals with outside parties, it would have to disclose its status and say which Core or Cell it acts for. Statutory implied terms would limit counterparties to claims against the contracting Core or Cell, and would require them to return assets that belong to another Core or Cell. Transactions between parts of the same PCC would be allowed if necessary, on arm's length terms and consistent with segregation.

Governance, insolvency and tax

The summary says governance standards would follow the Companies Act, including a requirement for at least one Singapore-resident director, and that the name would include the words PCC or Protected Cell Company. A PCC would need an annual audit by a registered public accountant, with the finances of the Core and each Cell kept separate. Audited financial statements and the register of members would be publicly accessible.

On insolvency, the proposal builds on the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018. Each Cell could be wound up as if it were a separate legal person without affecting the rest of the PCC, and the PCC as a whole could be dissolved only once it no longer carries on insurance business. On tax, a PCC would be a single entity, goods and services tax would apply at Cell level, and each Cell would be treated as a separate person for stamp duty. Existing anti-money laundering requirements for licensed insurers would apply, and PCCs would need to keep accurate beneficial ownership information aligned with international standards.

The legislative path

The law firm notes that MAS plans a new PCC Act, with changes to the Insurance Act 1966, in two phases. The first consultation covers policy proposals, and a second would cover the draft Act and subsidiary legislation. The MAS release does not give a timetable after the consultation closed on August 7. Our sources also do not set out licensing steps, minimum capital or who may own a Cell, which readers will need to check in the full consultation paper.

What it could mean

For multinational companies, a PCC could offer a lower-cost way to manage group risks through a captive. For insurers and reinsurers, it could simplify the issuing of catastrophe-linked instruments. For governments, it could provide a legal home for shared disaster funds. Singapore is not the first financial centre to consider cell structures, but the details of MAS's rules, once final, will determine how competitive they are, and this article does not compare them with other jurisdictions because our sources do not.

What to watch next

Readers should watch for MAS publishing a response to the feedback it received, and for the second consultation on the draft legislation. The consultation paper and media release are on the MAS website. This article summarizes a proposal and public commentary and is not legal, tax or financial advice.
source_name: Monetary Authority of Singapore (media release and consultation paper, July 7, 2026); Rajah & Tann Asia (July 22, 2026)

key_points: The Monetary Authority of Singapore issued a consultation paper on July 7, 2026 proposing a legal framework for Protected Cell Companies, with comments due by August 7, 2026.
A PCC is a single legal entity made up of a Core and one or more Cells, with each Cell's assets and liabilities legally separate from other Cells and from the Core.

The initial uses are captive insurance, including rent-a-captive arrangements, insurance-linked securities issued from Cells without a new special purpose vehicle for each deal, and sovereign risk pools.

A law firm summary says the plan would create a new PCC Act with amendments to the Insurance Act 1966, and that a second consultation would cover the draft legislation.
why_it_matters: Companies, insurers and governments use captives, catastrophe bonds and risk pools to cover risks that the standard insurance market prices high or will not cover. If Singapore makes it cheaper to set up ring-fenced structures, more of that activity could be run from Asia, which matters in a region where most disaster losses are uninsured.

title: The FCA's Mills Review Expects AI to Move Retail Finance From Human-Led to Delegated Services and Makes Seven Priority Recommendations, Keeping the Consumer Duty at the Core
summary: The Financial Conduct Authority published the Mills Review on July 6, 2026, an independent review led by Sheldon Mills of how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030 and beyond; it identifies four systemic shifts, judges the current outcomes-based regime broadly fit for purpose and makes seven priority recommendations.
description:
On July 6, 2026, the UK Financial Conduct Authority published The Mills Review, a report on how artificial intelligence could change retail financial services over the coming years. The report is based on an independent review led by Sheldon Mills, the FCA's Executive Director for Consumers and Competition, and looks ahead to 2030 and beyond. This article is based on a summary published by the law firm A&O Shearman, not on the FCA's full text, so it covers the headline conclusions and recommendations and says plainly where detail is missing. The summary did not include any direct quotation from Mr Mills, details of what the FCA will do next, or a timetable.

The central conclusion

The review's main finding, in the words quoted in the summary, is that AI is likely to drive a transition from human-led financial activity to increasingly AI-enabled and delegated services. Two parts of that sentence matter. First, firms are expected to embed AI across many of their functions, not just in customer-facing chat tools. Second, consumers are expected to use AI tools and agents to manage their finances, which means that software could compare products, switch accounts or make payments on a person's behalf. The word delegated is important: if a customer hands a decision to an AI agent, questions arise about who is responsible when the outcome is poor.

Four systemic shifts

The review groups its analysis into four shifts. The summary lists them as headings, and the one-line glosses below are general explanations of the terms rather than the review's own findings.

AI becoming central to how firms operate. Instead of being an add-on, AI would be part of underwriting, credit assessment, fraud detection, servicing and decision-making.

AI-led consumer journeys. More of the path from a customer's question to a purchase would run through AI-driven interfaces, possibly operated by third parties instead of the financial firm.

Changes to competition and market power. The summary lists this as a shift without giving detail. The specifics are in the full report.

Greater financial crime and cyber risk. AI can be used by criminals as well as by firms, and more automated, connected systems create more points of attack.

The existing framework

One of the more notable conclusions is that the review does not call for the existing rulebook to be thrown out. It considers the current outcomes-based regime broadly fit for purpose. That regime includes the Consumer Duty, which requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers; the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, which makes named senior individuals accountable for areas of a firm's business; and operational resilience requirements, which set expectations for firms to withstand disruption. The review says these tools need to evolve to keep pace with AI, rather than being replaced.

The seven priority recommendations

According to the summary, which paraphrases them, the recommendations are:

First, secure and adapt the regulatory perimeter. The perimeter is the boundary that decides which activities need FCA authorisation. If AI agents and platforms start to perform activities that are close to regulated advice or distribution, the boundary may need to be reviewed.

Second, strengthen system-wide coordination and oversight. AI affects competition, data, cyber security and consumer protection, which sit with different authorities, so the review calls for better coordination.

Third, monitor the move toward autonomous models and adapt rules accordingly. The summary does not say how autonomy is currently distributed.

Fourth, scale up the FCA's AI Lab, the regulator's programme for engaging with AI developers and firms.

Fifth, enable the foundations for agentic finance, meaning the standards and infrastructure needed for AI agents to act safely for consumers.

Sixth, build and adopt an AI-enabled, agentic supervisory model, so that the regulator itself uses AI in supervising firms.

Seventh, develop a trusted, public-interest AI-enabled financial capability service, which would help consumers make better decisions with AI support.

The explanations added to the recommendations above are general descriptions of the terms, not statements of what the review says in detail; the summary lists the titles only.

What is missing and what to watch

The summary does not say how the FCA will respond to the recommendations, whether legislation or rule changes would be needed, or who will take each action. It also does not describe what the review says about accountability when an AI agent makes a mistake, which is probably the question that matters most to consumers. The report also looks to 2030, so many of its predictions are expectations rather than present facts, and the summary notes no caveats about uncertainty.

For firms, the practical message is that the regulator is likely to keep applying the Consumer Duty and senior manager accountability to AI-driven services, and to expect firms to understand and control the systems they use. For consumers, the review does not change rights today. Anyone who uses an AI tool for financial decisions should check who is providing the service and whether it is a regulated firm. Readers who need the exact recommendations should consult the FCA's published report. This article is general information and not legal advice.
source_name: A&O Shearman FinReg (summary of the FCA's Mills Review, published July 6, 2026)
image_alt: Artificial intelligence and data systems in financial services (illustrative)
key_points: The FCA published the Mills Review on July 6, 2026; it is based on an independent review led by Sheldon Mills, the FCA's Executive Director for Consumers and Competition, of how AI could affect retail financial services by 2030 and beyond.

Its core conclusion is that AI is likely to drive a transition from human-led financial activity to increasingly AI-enabled and delegated services, with consumers using AI tools and agents to manage their finances.
It identifies four systemic shifts: AI becoming central to how firms operate, AI-led consumer journeys, changes to competition and market power, and greater financial crime and cyber risk.

The review considers the current outcomes-based regime, including the Consumer Duty, the Senior Managers and Certification Regime and operational resilience rules, broadly fit for purpose but in need of evolving as AI advances.

Its seven priority recommendations cover the regulatory perimeter, system-wide coordination, monitoring autonomous models, scaling the FCA's AI Lab, foundations for agentic finance, an AI-enabled supervisory model and a public-interest financial capability service.
why_it_matters: Banks, insurers and investment firms in the UK are already using AI, and consumers are starting to ask AI tools to compare products and manage money. The review shows the direction the UK regulator is thinking in: keep the existing outcomes-based rules, but adapt perimeter, coordination and supervision for a world in which software acts on a customer's behalf.

title: French Insurers' €2.85 Trillion Portfolio Absorbed €33.7 Billion of Valuation Losses in Q1 2026 as Long-Term Rates Rose, Offsetting Almost All New Investment
summary: Banque de France data show French insurers and pension funds held €2,854.5 billion of financial investments at end-Q1 2026; net inflows of €34.9 billion were offset by €33.7 billion of valuation losses from rising long-term rates, and a look-through view shows 26% of holdings are equities.
description:
French insurers and pension funds ended the first quarter of 2026 with financial investments of €2,854.5 billion, but a rise in long-term interest rates meant that almost all of their new investment was cancelled out on paper by falling asset values. The figures come from the Banque de France, which published its quarterly statistics on the financial investments of insurance corporations and pension funds on July 7, 2026 (updated July 17). The next publication was scheduled for October 6, 2026.

The headline arithmetic is simple. Insurers made net investments of €32.7 billion in the quarter, and pension funds added €2.2 billion, a combined €34.9 billion of new money. Against that, valuation effects were -€33.7 billion. The Banque de France attributes the valuation losses to rising long-term rates, which lowered bond prices, and to falling share prices. In other words, the portfolio barely grew in value over the quarter even though a great deal of fresh money was invested.

The breakdown by segment shows where the effect fell. Life and composite insurers, which hold most of the money because they manage life insurance savings and retirement products, held €2,354.0 billion at the end of the quarter. They invested €29.5 billion net but suffered valuation effects of -€28.6 billion. Non-life insurers, which write car, home and commercial cover, held €299.1 billion, with net flows of €3.2 billion and valuations of -€2.5 billion. Pension funds held €201.3 billion, with net flows of €2.2 billion and valuations of -€2.6 billion. The loss is therefore concentrated in the life segment, simply because that is where the assets are.

What did insurers buy? Before applying the look-through approach, the Banque de France reports direct purchases of long-term debt securities of €20.9 billion. Insurers also put €14.4 billion into investment fund shares, including €8.3 billion into non-money-market funds. Net flows into listed shares were -€2 billion, meaning insurers were net sellers. The pattern suggests a preference for fixed income at a time when bond yields were rising, which allows new money to lock in higher returns, together with continued use of funds as a way to gain diversified exposure.

The look-through view gives a fuller picture of what the portfolio holds. French funds are a major route for insurers' investments, so the Banque de France applies a look-through approach, treating the securities inside French funds as if the insurer held them directly. This changes the picture a good deal. The share of equities rises from 10% to 26% of the total, and the share of debt securities from 50% to 64%. About 1% remains in fund units that cannot be looked through, mainly foreign funds. By issuer, about 40% of the portfolio consists of securities issued by the financial sector excluding mutual funds, split between 25% other financial institutions and 15% monetary financial institutions such as banks. Geographically, about 41% of the securities are issued in France and 41% abroad, with the remaining 18% being fund units that cannot be allocated.

The banks-and-insurers link is worth noting. A large part of insurers' holdings are claims on the financial sector, so the health of banks and insurers is interconnected, which is a recurrent theme in financial-stability analysis. The source does not discuss that risk, but the data show its scale.

A methodology note affects how the series should be read. From the first quarter of 2025, the series includes an estimate of foreign fund holdings, which reduces the unallocated share of fund units. The scope also now covers directly held deposits and loans and indirect real estate holdings through funds. Comparisons with older data should take this into account.

How should readers interpret valuation losses? A valuation loss is a change in the market value of assets that insurers still hold, not cash lost. For a life insurer holding bonds to maturity to meet long-term obligations, a fall in market price does not necessarily mean a realised loss, because the bond will still pay its coupons and its face value at maturity unless the issuer defaults. Rising rates also allow insurers to reinvest maturing bonds and new premiums at higher yields, which supports future returns and the ability to pay guaranteed or declared returns on policies. The downside is that higher rates can encourage policyholders to move savings elsewhere, and if insurers had to sell bonds at a loss to meet withdrawals, the paper losses would become real. The Banque de France data do not indicate that this occurred, and they only record asset values and flows.

For French savers, the main route to this market is life insurance, a very popular savings product in France. The returns credited to policyholders depend partly on what insurers earn on their portfolios, so persistent increases in interest rates feed through gradually as insurers reinvest. The data do not address policyholder returns or surrenders, so no conclusion can be drawn on those from this release alone.

For the wider economy, French insurers are significant buyers of government and corporate debt, and also fund companies through equity. Net purchases of €20.9 billion of long-term debt in a single quarter show how much they contribute to financing. Weaker prices for existing holdings do not stop them from buying; in fact, higher yields may make debt more attractive.

The October 6 publication will show whether valuation effects reversed or deepened in the second quarter, depending on how rates and share prices moved. Readers following the French insurance sector can use these quarterly statistics as a simple way to see how rate moves translate into portfolio values.
source_name: Banque de France (Financial investments of insurance corporations and pension funds, Q1 2026, published July 7, 2026)
image_alt: Paris financial district representing French insurers (illustrative)
key_points: French insurers and pension funds held €2,854.5 billion of financial investments at the end of Q1 2026, according to the Banque de France.

Net flows were €32.7 billion for insurers and €2.2 billion for pension funds, but valuation effects of -€33.7 billion, driven by rising long-term rates and falling share prices, almost cancelled them out.
Life and composite insurers held €2,354.0 billion (valuation effect -€28.6 billion), non-life insurers €299.1 billion (-€2.5 billion) and pension funds €201.3 billion (-€2.6 billion).
Insurers bought €20.9 billion of long-term debt securities and €14.4 billion of investment fund shares, while net listed shares were -€2 billion.
On a look-through basis, 64% of holdings are debt securities and 26% equities, with about 41% issued in France and 41% abroad.
why_it_matters: French insurers are among Europe's largest institutional investors, and the savings of millions of households sit in their portfolios. When rates rise, bond values drop on paper even as new money earns higher yields, so these figures show how interest-rate moves feed through to life insurance returns and to the funds insurers lend to governments and companies.
